title: Making mead from surplus honey
subtitle: A basic still mead from honey, water, and wine yeast.
excerpt: Mead is fermented honey and water: one of the oldest alcoholic drinks and a natural use for uncapped or granulated honey that cannot be sold. A simple 4.5-litre batch needs 1 to 1.5 kg of honey, a glass demijohn, an airlock, and wine yeast. It is ready to taste in 6 to 8 weeks and improves significantly with 6 months' ageing.
sourceNotes: C.J.J. Berry, First Steps in Winemaking (11th edn., 1987), mead chapter. Ken Schramm, The Compleat Meadmaker (2003). Andrew Lea, Craft Cider Making (4th edn., 2015), fermentation chapter (applied to mead).

glossaryTerms.definition: The mixture of honey and water before fermentation starts. The term is borrowed from winemaking.
A supplement added to honey must to provide nitrogen and vitamins that wine yeast needs. Honey is deficient in yeast nutrients, making additions important for a reliable fermentation.

content.text: Mead fermentation converts the natural sugars in honey into alcohol and carbon dioxide. The process is slower than brewing beer, because honey must has very low nutrient levels for yeast. Adding yeast nutrient and keeping the temperature in the right range (18 to 22 C) is the most important thing you can do for a reliable result.
1 to 1.5 kg honey (1 kg for a dry mead; 1.5 kg for a sweeter, stronger result)
4 litres water, cooled to room temperature
1 sachet (5 g) white wine yeast (Lalvin 71B or EC-1118 work well)
Optional: 1 Campden tablet (a sulphite steriliser) to kill wild yeasts before adding the wine yeast

Warm the honey slightly to make it liquid if it has granulated. Do not boil honey for mead; modern practice favours a no-heat approach that preserves aromatics. Dissolve the honey in 2 litres of lukewarm water (under 40 C) in the demijohn.
Top up to 4.5 litres with the remaining cooled water. Add yeast nutrient and stir to combine. This is your
If using a Campden tablet, add it at this point, seal the demijohn with a bung, and leave for 24 hours before adding yeast. If not using Campden, proceed immediately.
Rehydrate the yeast sachet in 100 ml warm water (30 C) for 15 minutes. Add to the must. Fit the
filled with cooled boiled water. Place in a warm spot (18 to 22 C).

Active fermentation (bubbling through the airlock) usually starts within 24 to 48 hours. Fermentation slows and stops over 4 to 6 weeks. The mead is ready to rack (transfer off the lees) when the airlock is producing fewer than one bubble per minute.
Siphon into a clean demijohn, leaving the sediment behind. Fit a fresh airlock and leave for a further 4 to 6 weeks. Rack a second time if more sediment forms. Bottle once clear.

A brewing hydrometer measures the specific gravity (SG) of the must. Take a reading before adding yeast (original gravity) and again when fermentation stops (final gravity). The difference tells you the alcohol content: a drop of 0.070 SG equates to approximately 9% ABV. This is useful but not essential for a home batch you are making for personal consumption.

attrs.cue: No bubbling from the airlock after 72 hours
attrs.cause: Airlock not sealed properly, yeast did not rehydrate, or must temperature is below 15 C
attrs.fix: Check the airlock seal. Check the room temperature. Add a second sachet of rehydrated yeast if there is still no activity after 96 hours.

attrs.cue: Mead tastes sharp and unpleasant after 8 weeks
attrs.cause: Still fermenting, or a stuck fermentation with residual off-flavours
attrs.fix: Take an SG reading. If still falling, it is still working. If stable and high (above 1.015), fermentation may be stuck; add more nutrient and a fresh yeast starter. Mead that smells of vinegar has been contaminated with acetobacter and should be discarded.
